blocks.title: Business Understanding
blocks.body:
The first stage of the AI lifecycle asks two distinct questions. First: is AI even the right approach to this problem - or would a simpler, non-AI solution (a fixed rule, a checklist, an unchanged human process) do the job with less risk and complexity? Only once that's answered does the second question arise: if AI genuinely is appropriate, should this particular system, as currently conceived, actually be built?

This is where ethical thinking has the greatest impact. Decisions made here - about whether AI is the right tool at all, what problem to solve, what data to use, how to measure success - shape everything that follows. Rushing this stage without ethical consideration risks building systems that may cause harm.

blocks.title: If you use AI tools rather than build them
blocks.body: Not everyone taking this course decides whether an AI system gets built - plenty of us just use tools, like Copilot, that someone else already built and rolled out. That doesn't make this stage irrelevant to you. Knowing the questions a responsible team should have asked - was AI actually the right tool here, who could this harm, how was 'success' defined - gives you a basis for judging how much to trust a tool's output, and for raising a concern if something about how it's used (or could be used) doesn't sit right.

blocks.title: The frameworks suggest...
blocks.body:
The EU AI Act requires organisations to consider potential risks before deploying AI systems, with higher-risk applications subject to stricter requirements. It classifies AI systems into four risk levels: unacceptable risk (prohibited), high risk (heavily regulated), limited risk (transparency obligations), and minimal risk.

ISO 42001, the international standard for AI management systems, recommends that organisations establish clear accountability from the outset - including defining the intended purpose and potential harms of any AI project before development begins. Unlike the EU AI Act or UK GDPR, ISO 42001 is a voluntary, certifiable standard rather than law - organisations choose to adopt and be audited against it, rather than being legally required to.

items.title: Clarifying the problem
items.body: Before any AI project begins, it is essential to justify why AI - rather than a simpler rule-based system, an unchanged manual process, or no intervention at all - is the right solution. What problem are you actually solving, and could it be addressed another way, with less risk and less complexity? An AI Impact Assessment documents the intended use, potential benefits and possible harms - including the live possibility that the right answer is not to build an AI system at all - ensuring these questions are answered before resources are committed.

items.title: Weighing the benefit
items.body: Risk assessment needs an equal and opposite step: naming the benefit clearly enough to test it. Who benefits, how significant is that benefit, and for which groups - including people who won't use the system directly, but are still affected by it? A benefit that's vague, marginal, or accrues to a different group than the one bearing the risk is a signal to pause, not proceed.

items.title: Defining success ethically
items.body: Success metrics should go beyond technical performance. A model that is 95% accurate overall may still perform poorly for specific groups. Ethical success criteria ask: is the system fair across different populations? Are there groups who might be disproportionately harmed by errors? Defining this upfront creates accountability.

items.title: Stakeholder considerations
items.body: Who will be affected by this AI system? Engaging a diverse range of stakeholders - including those who will be subject to AI-driven decisions - helps surface ethical concerns that a homogeneous project team might miss. This includes employees, customers, marginalised communities and wider society.

items.title: Ask yourself
items.body:
• Is AI actually the right approach here - or would a simpler rule, process or human judgement work with less risk?
  • If AI is appropriate, should this particular system, as currently designed, be built?
  • Have we articulated who benefits from this system, and how significantly - not just who could be harmed?
  • Have we identified who could be harmed by this system?
  • Have we defined success in a way that includes fairness, not just accuracy?
  • Have we engaged the people who will be affected by this system?

blocks.title: Risk categorisation under the EU AI Act

items.title: Unacceptable risk
items.body: Some AI applications are prohibited outright under the EU AI Act. These include social scoring systems used by governments to evaluate citizens, AI that uses subliminal or manipulative techniques to distort someone's behaviour in harmful ways or that exploits vulnerabilities linked to age or disability, and most uses of real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces.
items.graphicAlt: A prohibition symbol - a circle with a diagonal line through it

items.title: High risk
items.body: High-risk AI systems include those used in critical infrastructure, education, employment, access to essential services, law enforcement, migration and the administration of justice. These must meet strict requirements around accuracy, transparency, oversight and documentation.
items.graphicAlt: A warning triangle with an exclamation mark

items.title: Limited and minimal risk
items.body: Many AI systems fall into lower risk categories. Chatbots and AI-generated content carry transparency obligations - users must know they are interacting with AI. Most AI, such as spam filters and recommendation systems, is minimal risk and subject only to general requirements.
items.graphicAlt: A shield with a checkmark inside it

blocks.title: Case study: The A-level algorithm
blocks.body:
In 2020, with A-level exams cancelled due to COVID-19, the UK government used a statistical algorithm to award grades to students. The algorithm was designed to be 'fair' at a population level - but it was systematically unfair to individual students.

The system used schools' historical performance as a key factor. Students at schools with lower historical attainment had their predicted grades downgraded, regardless of individual ability. Students at private schools - historically higher-performing - were largely unaffected.

Grades were reversed within days following widespread protest. The episode became a defining case study in algorithmic impact assessment and accountability.

blocks.title: What was the central ethical problem with the A-level grading algorithm?
blocks.instruction: Select one option, then select Submit.

items.text: Statistical methods should never be used for any kind of academic grading decision.
items.feedback: Not quite. The issue wasn't that statistics were used at all - a well-designed statistical approach could have avoided penalising individual students for their school's history.

items.text: It could produce unfair outcomes for individual students based on their school's historical results.
The algorithm's underlying mathematics was too complex for educators to understand.
items.feedback: Not quite. Complexity wasn't the problem - plenty of complex statistical models are used responsibly. The issue was the specific factor it relied on: school-level historical performance.

items.text: Cancelling that year's exams because of COVID-19 was itself the wrong decision to make.
items.feedback: Not quite. Cancelling exams during a pandemic wasn't itself controversial. The controversy was in how grades were then estimated, and the unfair effect that had on individual students.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. An AI Impact Assessment at the Business Understanding stage should have modelled outcomes across different groups of students. The disproportionate impact on students at lower-performing schools was knowable in advance - it should have been built into the system's ethical success criteria from the start.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. An AI Impact Assessment should have modelled potential outcomes across different groups. The disproportionate impact on students at lower-performing schools was predictable - it should have been part of the ethical success criteria for the system from the outset.

blocks.title: Coming up...
blocks.body: Once you've decided to build an AI system, the next stage is Data Acquisition and Understanding. The data used to train your AI is one of the most powerful determinants of whether it behaves fairly - or replicates and amplifies existing inequalities.
